intro: Every day, your body meets germs too small to see. Most of the time, you never notice. Your skin, your immune system and simple habits like handwashing keep you well. Sometimes a germ gets through, and you catch a cold or a fever.

People have learned a lot about germs over hundreds of years. A country doctor named Edward Jenner made the first vaccine. Scientists found antibiotics. Health workers around the world worked together to wipe out smallpox.

In this unit, you will learn how germs spread and how your body fights back. You will also learn first aid for small hurts, when to call 911, and how to stay calm and get a trusted adult. You can be a real helper.
bigQuestion: How do our bodies, science and our own actions keep us and the people around us safe and well?

title: Germs, Vaccines and First Aid

chapters.title: Germs and How We Fight Them
chapters.bigQuestion: Germs are too small to see, so how do our bodies, our habits and our medicines keep us well?

story.title: The Milkmaid's Clear Skin
story.kicker: An old country story helped a doctor find a way to stop one of the worst sicknesses in history.
paragraphs: Long ago in the English countryside, a sickness called smallpox scared almost everyone. It gave people a high fever and bumpy spots all over the skin. Many people died from it. Many who got well had scars on their faces for life.

Edward Jenner was a country doctor in the village of Berkeley, England. Farm families there told an old story. They said milkmaids who caught a mild sickness from cows almost never got smallpox. That cow sickness was called cowpox. It gave a milkmaid a few sores on her hands, and then she got well.

One well-known telling says a young milkmaid spoke to Jenner herself. She said she would never catch smallpox, because she had already had cowpox. Nobody knows her exact words. But Jenner kept thinking about the idea. Could a mild cow sickness protect a person from a deadly one?

In 1796 Jenner decided to test it. He took a little matter from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. He put it into a small cut on the arm of an eight-year-old boy, James Phipps. James got a little sick and then got better.

Weeks later, Jenner exposed James to smallpox. James did not get sick. Jenner tested more people and wrote down what he saw. His work led to the first vaccine. Doctors today would never test on a child that way, but his idea changed the world.
story.think: Jenner heard a story, then tested it. Why is it important to test an idea instead of just believing a story?

lessons.title: Bacteria Are Tiny Living Things
lessons.mainIdea: Bacteria are tiny one-celled living things; most are harmless or helpful, but a few can make us sick.
reading: Think about a spoonful of yogurt. It is full of living things, too small to see. They are called *bacteria*. Each one is just a single cell. You would need a microscope to see them.
Bacteria live almost everywhere. They live in soil, in water and on your skin. Millions live inside your gut. Most bacteria do not hurt you. Many help you digest food or turn milk into yogurt.
A few kinds of bacteria are *germs*. A germ is a tiny living thing that can make you sick. One kind of bacteria causes strep throat. Another kind can get into a cut and make it red and sore.

words.d: tiny living things made of just one cell; most are harmless, and a few cause sickness
tiny living things, like some bacteria and viruses, that can make you sick

look.title: A Look Through a Microscope
look.text: A student puts a drop of pond water under a microscope. At first she sees nothing. Then she turns the knob. Tiny rods and dots appear, far too small to see with her eyes alone.
look.prompt: Why did people not know about bacteria until they had microscopes?

check.why: The reading says bacteria are tiny living things made of just one cell.

check.why: The reading names strep throat as a sickness caused by bacteria.

lessons.title: Viruses Need a Host
lessons.mainIdea: Viruses are even smaller than bacteria, and they can only make more of themselves inside a living cell.
reading: When you catch a cold, a *virus* is usually the cause. A virus is a germ even smaller than bacteria. The flu and chickenpox are also caused by viruses.

A virus cannot grow or make copies on its own. It must get inside a living cell. The cell it uses is called the *host*. Inside, the virus makes the cell build many new viruses. Then they spread to more cells.
Bacteria and viruses are both germs, but they are different. Bacteria are living cells. Viruses are much smaller and are not cells at all. This difference matters when doctors choose a medicine.

words.d: a very tiny germ that can only make copies of itself inside a living cell
the living thing or cell that a virus uses to make copies of itself

look.title: How Small Are Germs?
look.prompt: About how many bacteria could line up across one hair? Which germ is the smallest?

check.q: What must a virus do to make copies of itself?
choices: Split in half on its own
check.why: A virus can only make copies inside a living cell, its host.

check.q: Which is usually caused by a virus?
check.why: The reading says colds are usually caused by viruses.

check.q: How are viruses different from bacteria?
choices: Viruses are much smaller and are not cells.
check.why: Bacteria are living cells; viruses are much smaller and are not cells.

lessons.title: How Germs Travel
lessons.mainIdea: Germs spread through the air, by touch, and in food and water, so washing hands and covering coughs help.
reading: Maya sneezes into the air. Tiny drops fly out. If she has a cold, the drops carry the virus. A friend nearby can breathe them in. That is one way germs *spread*.

Germs also spread by touch. Someone coughs into a hand, then touches a door handle. The next person touches it and then rubs an eye. Germs can also ride in food that was not cooked well, or in dirty water.

Simple habits block these paths. Wash hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds. Cough or sneeze into your elbow. Keep food clean and cooked. Drink clean water. These habits cut down the chances of getting sick. This is called good *hygiene*.

words.d: to pass from one person or place to another
habits that keep you and others clean and healthy, like washing hands

look.title: Washing Hands the Right Way
look.text: Wet your hands with clean running water. Add soap and rub every part, including the backs and between the fingers, for at least 20 seconds. Rinse well and dry with a clean towel or air dry.
look.cite: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), When and How to Wash Your Hands, handwashing guidance
look.prompt: Why do you think the CDC says to scrub for 20 seconds and not just a quick splash?

check.q: Which is one way germs spread?
check.why: Sneezes send out tiny drops that can carry germs through the air.

check.q: How long should you scrub hands with soap?
check.why: The reading and the CDC say to scrub for about 20 seconds.

check.q: Where is the best place to sneeze if you have no tissue?
check.why: Sneezing into your elbow keeps germs off your hands and out of the air.

lessons.title: White Blood Cells on Guard
lessons.mainIdea: The immune system uses white blood cells to find and destroy germs that get into the body.
reading: Your skin is like a wall that keeps most germs out. But sometimes germs get in, like through a scrape on your knee. Then your body has a team ready to fight. That team is your *immune system*.

The fighters are *white blood cells*. They travel in your blood to where germs are. Some white blood cells swallow germs whole. Others make *antibodies*. Antibodies are like tags that stick to a germ so other cells can find it and destroy it.

Your immune system also remembers. After it beats a germ, some cells keep a memory of it. If the same germ comes back, your body can fight it faster. This memory is why many people get chickenpox only once.

words.d: the body's team of cells and organs that fights germs
blood cells that find and fight germs
tiny tags the body makes that stick to one kind of germ so it can be destroyed

look.title: The Scraped Knee
look.text: Leo scrapes his knee on the playground. The next day the spot is a little pink and warm. A few days later it has healed. Under the skin, white blood cells rushed in to clean up germs.
look.prompt: What was happening inside Leo's knee while it healed?

check.q: What is the job of white blood cells?
choices: To carry food to the stomach
check.why: White blood cells travel to germs and fight them.

check.q: What do antibodies do?
choices: Stick to a germ so it can be destroyed
check.why: Antibodies are like tags that stick to one kind of germ.

check.q: Why do many people get chickenpox only once?
choices: The immune system remembers the germ.
check.why: The immune system keeps a memory of germs it has beaten and fights them faster next time.

lessons.title: A Fever Is a Fight
lessons.mainIdea: A fever is a higher body temperature that often means the immune system is fighting germs.
reading: Ana wakes up hot and tired. Her dad checks her with a thermometer. Her temperature is higher than usual. She has a *fever*.

A fever is not a germ. It is one way your body fights germs. When germs get in, the body turns up its heat. Many germs do not grow as well in a warmer body. The heat also helps the immune system work.
A fever can make you feel tired and achy. Resting and drinking water help. Tell a grown-up when you feel hot or sick. A grown-up can check your *temperature* and call a doctor or nurse if needed.

words.d: a body temperature higher than usual, often a sign the body is fighting germs
how hot or cold something is, measured with a thermometer

look.title: Reading a Thermometer
look.cite: CDC definition of fever (100.4 °F or higher); typical body temperature from common medical references
look.prompt: Ana's thermometer says 101. Does she have a fever? How do you know?

check.q: What is a fever?
choices: A body temperature higher than usual
check.why: A fever is a higher body temperature, often from fighting germs.

check.q: How can a fever help the body?
choices: Many germs do not grow as well in the heat.
check.why: The reading says many germs grow less well in a warmer body.

check.q: What should Ana do when she feels hot and sick?
check.why: Telling a grown-up and resting are the helpful steps in the reading.

lessons.title: How a Vaccine Works
lessons.mainIdea: A vaccine teaches the immune system to know a germ, so the body is ready before the real germ arrives.
reading: A fire drill helps you practice before there is a real fire. A *vaccine* is like a drill for your immune system. It lets the body practice fighting a germ without getting very sick.
A vaccine holds a weak, dead or harmless piece of a germ, or instructions for making one. It is often given as a shot. The immune system sees it and makes antibodies. It also makes memory cells.

Later, the real germ may come. Now the body knows it. It can fight fast, often before you feel sick. This protection is called *immunity*. Your doctor or nurse can tell you which vaccines you need and when.

words.d: a medicine, often a shot, that teaches the immune system to know a germ
the body's protection against a germ it already knows

look.title: The Practice Drill
look.text: At school, the fire alarm rings for a drill. Everyone walks out in a line. There is no fire. A month later, the class does it again, faster and calmer.
look.prompt: How is a fire drill like a vaccine? How is it different?

check.q: What does a vaccine do?
choices: Teaches the immune system to know a germ
Kills every germ in a room
check.why: A vaccine lets the immune system learn a germ before the real one comes.

check.q: What does a vaccine usually hold?
choices: A weak, dead or harmless piece of a germ, or instructions for one
check.why: The reading says vaccines hold a weak, dead or harmless part of a germ, or instructions to make one.

check.q: What is immunity?
choices: The body's protection against a germ it knows
check.why: Immunity is the body's protection against a germ it has learned.

lessons.title: Edward Jenner Tests an Idea
lessons.mainIdea: In 1796 Edward Jenner used cowpox to protect a boy from smallpox, which led to the first vaccine.
reading: *Smallpox* was a sickness caused by a virus. It killed many people for thousands of years. In the 1700s, English farm families noticed something. Milkmaids who had caught *cowpox* from cows seemed safe from smallpox.
Edward Jenner, a country doctor, tested this idea in 1796. He put matter from a cowpox sore into a cut on James Phipps's arm. Later, he exposed James to smallpox. James stayed well.
Jenner wrote a book about his tests in 1798. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Today, doctors test vaccines with careful rules to keep volunteers safe.

words.d: a deadly sickness caused by a virus that gave people fever and spots
a mild sickness from cows that protected people from smallpox

look.title: Jenner's Report
look.text: Jenner wrote that people who had caught cowpox from milking cows seemed to be protected from smallpox afterward. He described giving cowpox to a boy and then showing that the boy did not catch smallpox.
look.cite: Edward Jenner, An Inquiry into the Causes and Effects of the Variolae Vaccinae, 1798
look.prompt: What did Jenner see, and what did he do to test it?

check.q: What did Jenner use to protect James Phipps?
check.why: Jenner used matter from a cowpox sore to protect James.

check.q: When did Jenner test his idea on James?
check.why: Jenner's test on James Phipps was in 1796.

check.q: Where does the word vaccine come from?
check.why: Vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow.

lessons.title: The End of Smallpox
lessons.mainIdea: Vaccines used all over the world wiped out smallpox, and in 1980 it was declared gone.
reading: After Jenner, many countries began to vaccinate people against smallpox. In 1967 the World Health Organization started a big push to end it everywhere. Health workers traveled to villages all over the world.
The workers found each new case. Then they vaccinated everyone around that sick person. This stopped the virus from finding new people. The last natural case was found in Somalia, in Africa, in 1977.
In 1980 the World Health Organization said smallpox was *eradicated*. That means it was wiped out in the wild. It is the first human disease ever wiped out. It took teamwork from many *nations*.

words.d: wiped out completely, so it no longer spreads anywhere
countries with their own governments

look.title: The World Says Smallpox Is Gone
look.text: In 1980 the World Health Assembly declared that the world and all its peoples had won freedom from smallpox. It thanked the nations and health workers who took part.
look.cite: World Health Assembly, resolution declaring the global eradication of smallpox, May 1980
look.prompt: Why do you think this was called a win for all the world's peoples?

check.q: What does eradicated mean?
check.why: Eradicated means wiped out so it no longer spreads.

check.q: In what year was smallpox declared gone?
check.why: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

check.q: How did health workers stop smallpox from spreading?
choices: They told people to stay in the sun.
They found each case and vaccinated people nearby.
check.why: Workers found cases and vaccinated people around them, so the virus ran out of new people.

lessons.title: Antibiotics Fight Bacteria
lessons.mainIdea: Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing.
reading: In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming came back to his lab in London. He saw mold growing on a dish of bacteria. Around the mold, the bacteria had died. The mold made something that killed them.

That something became *penicillin*. It was one of the first *antibiotics*. An antibiotic is a medicine that kills bacteria or stops them from growing. Penicillin was made in large amounts in the 1940s and saved many lives.
Doctors give antibiotics for infections caused by bacteria, like strep throat. Only a doctor or nurse can decide if you need one. Take it just the way they say, and finish it if they tell you to.

words.d: medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing
one of the first antibiotics, first found in a mold

look.title: The Moldy Dish
look.text: Fleming's dish had a spot of fuzzy mold. All around it was a clear ring where bacteria were gone. Farther away, the bacteria grew thick.
look.prompt: What clue told Fleming that the mold was doing something to the bacteria?

check.q: Who noticed mold killing bacteria in 1928?
check.why: Alexander Fleming saw the mold in his London lab in 1928.

check.q: What is an antibiotic?
choices: A shot that teaches the body a germ
A medicine that kills bacteria or stops their growth
check.why: Antibiotics are medicines that work against bacteria.

check.q: Who decides if you need an antibiotic?
check.why: Only a doctor or nurse can decide if you need one.

lessons.title: Why Antibiotics Skip Viruses
lessons.mainIdea: Antibiotics work on bacteria but not on viruses, so they do not help a cold or the flu.
reading: Sam has a runny nose and a cough. He asks his doctor for an antibiotic. The doctor kindly says no. Sam's cold is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not work on viruses.
Antibiotics attack parts that bacteria have, like their cell walls. Viruses do not have those parts. So the medicine has nothing to hit. For a cold, rest, fluids and time usually help most.

Using antibiotics when they are not needed can cause a problem. Some bacteria learn to survive them. This is called antibiotic *resistance*. Using antibiotics only when a doctor says so helps keep them *effective* for everyone.

words.d: when germs change so a medicine no longer works on them
able to do the job it is supposed to do

look.title: Fleming's Warning
look.text: When Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize, he warned that if people took too little penicillin or took it when it was not needed, bacteria could learn to resist it.
look.prompt: Fleming found penicillin. Why would he warn people about using it the wrong way?

check.q: Why did Sam's doctor not give him an antibiotic?
choices: His cold was caused by a virus.
check.why: Antibiotics do not work on viruses, and colds are caused by viruses.

check.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
choices: When bacteria can survive a medicine
check.why: Resistance means germs change so the medicine no longer works.

check.q: What helps most for a cold?
check.why: The reading says rest, fluids and time usually help a cold most.

review.why: Bacteria are one-celled living things; viruses are not cells.

review.q: Which habit helps stop germs from spreading by touch?
review.why: Handwashing with soap removes germs from your hands.

review.q: What part of the body fights germs with white blood cells?
review.why: The immune system uses white blood cells to fight germs.

review.q: What story gave Edward Jenner his idea?
choices: Children who ate yogurt stayed well.
Doctors who washed hands stayed well.
People in cities never got sick.

review.why: Farm families said milkmaids with cowpox did not catch smallpox.

review.why: Vaccines prepare the immune system; antibiotics attack bacteria during an infection.

choices: A sign the body is fighting germs
review.why: A fever is a higher temperature that often means the body is fighting.

review.q: Why should antibiotics be used only when a doctor says so?
review.why: Using them when not needed can help bacteria learn to survive them.

chapters.title: First Aid and Emergencies
chapters.bigQuestion: What can a young person do to help when someone is hurt or sick?

story.title: Rosa Makes the Call
story.kicker: When her grandfather fell, a ten-year-old girl remembered what to do.
paragraphs: Rosa was doing homework at the kitchen table. Her grandfather was in the next room, reaching for a box on a high shelf. Then she heard a loud thump. She ran in. Grandpa was on the floor. He was awake, but he could not get up, and his arm looked hurt.

Rosa's heart pounded. She wanted to cry. Then she remembered what her teacher had said: take a deep breath first. She breathed in slowly. She told Grandpa, "Stay still. I am getting help." No other grown-up was home.

Rosa picked up the phone and dialed 911. A calm voice asked, "What is your emergency?" Rosa said her grandfather fell and could not get up. She gave her home address, street and number, just the way she had practiced. She answered each question and did not hang up.
The helper on the phone told Rosa to unlock the front door and stay with Grandpa. Soon an ambulance arrived. The paramedics checked Grandpa and took him to the hospital to look at his arm.
Later, Grandpa squeezed Rosa's hand. "You stayed calm," he said. "You knew what to do." Rosa smiled. Knowing her address and practicing the call had made a real difference.
story.think: What did Rosa do first, before she made the call? Why did that help?

lessons.title: Cleaning a Small Cut
lessons.mainIdea: For a small cut, wash it with clean water, cover it with a bandage and tell an adult.
reading: Jada trips on the sidewalk and scrapes her hand. It stings, and there is a little blood. This is a small cut. Knowing a few steps helps her feel calm. Helping someone with a small hurt is called *first aid*.

First, wash the cut gently with clean water. Soap around the cut helps too. This rinses out dirt and germs. Next, press with a clean cloth if it is still bleeding. Then cover it with a *bandage* to keep it clean.
Always tell an adult about a cut. An adult can check it. A cut that is deep, will not stop bleeding, or gets red, puffy and warm later needs a doctor or nurse.

words.d: the first help given to someone who is hurt or sick, before a doctor arrives
a strip or pad that covers a cut to keep it clean

look.title: Jada's Three Steps
look.text: Jada's scraped hand has dirt in it. She goes inside. She rinses it under the faucet. She presses a clean cloth on it. Then she puts on a bandage and shows her mom.
look.prompt: Put Jada's steps in order in your own words. Which step keeps germs out?

check.q: What is the first step for a small cut?
choices: Wash it gently with clean water
check.why: Washing rinses out dirt and germs first.

check.q: Why do we cover a cut with a bandage?
check.why: A bandage keeps the cut clean.

check.q: Which cut needs a doctor or nurse?
choices: A tiny scratch that stopped bleeding
A deep cut that will not stop bleeding
A cut that is healing well
check.why: Deep cuts or cuts that will not stop bleeding need a doctor or nurse.

lessons.title: Helping a Nosebleed
lessons.mainIdea: For a nosebleed, sit up, lean forward and pinch the soft part of the nose.
reading: Ben is reading when his nose starts to bleed. Nosebleeds happen often, especially when the air is dry. Most stop on their own with the right care.

Ben sits up and leans a little *forward*. This keeps blood from running down his throat. He *pinches* the soft part of his nose, just below the hard bony part. He breathes through his mouth and keeps pinching for about 10 minutes.

Leaning back is an old habit, but it is not the best idea. Blood can go down the throat and upset the stomach. Ben tells an adult. If a nosebleed does not stop or came from a hard hit, an adult should get medical help.

words.d: toward the front
presses something tightly between the thumb and finger

look.title: Two Ways to Sit
look.text: Picture two kids with nosebleeds. One tips her head way back and looks at the ceiling. The other sits up, leans a little forward and pinches the soft part of his nose.
look.prompt: Which kid is doing it the helpful way? Explain why using the reading.

check.q: Which way should you lean for a nosebleed?
check.why: Leaning forward keeps blood from running down the throat.

check.q: Where should you pinch?
choices: The hard bony top of the nose
The soft part of the nose
check.why: The reading says to pinch the soft part, below the bony part.

check.q: Why is leaning back not a good idea?
choices: Blood can go down the throat.
check.why: Blood can run down the throat and upset the stomach.

lessons.title: Cooling a Burn
lessons.mainIdea: For a small burn, cool it under cool running water and tell an adult; do not use ice or butter.
reading: Mia touches a hot pan by mistake. Her finger turns red and hurts. This is a small *burn*. A burn is an injury from heat, like a stove, hot water or the sun.
The first step is to cool the burn. Hold it under *cool running water* for several minutes, until it feels better. Do not use ice. Ice can hurt the skin more. Do not put butter or oil on it either.
Tell an adult right away. An adult can cover a small burn loosely with a clean bandage. A big burn, a burn on the face, or a burn with blisters needs a doctor or nurse.

words.d: an injury to the skin from heat, fire, hot liquid or the sun
water from a faucet that is cool, not icy, used to cool a burn

look.title: What the Red Cross Teaches
look.text: For a small burn, stop the burning and cool it with cool running water. Do not use ice. Cover it loosely with a clean dressing. Get medical help for large or serious burns.
look.cite: American Red Cross, First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual (burn care guidance)
look.prompt: Which step in the Red Cross advice matches Mia's first step?

check.q: What should Mia do first for her burn?
choices: Cool it under cool running water
check.why: Cool running water is the first step for a small burn.

check.q: Why not use ice on a burn?
choices: Ice can hurt the skin more.
Ice spreads germs to the air.
check.why: The reading says ice can hurt the skin more.

check.q: Which burn needs a doctor or nurse?
choices: A tiny red spot that feels better
A big burn or one with blisters
check.why: Big burns, burns on the face and blistered burns need medical help.

lessons.title: When to Call 911
lessons.mainIdea: Call 911 when someone is in danger right now, like when they cannot breathe, will not wake up or is badly hurt.
reading: In the United States, 911 is the number to call in an *emergency*. An emergency is when someone is in danger right now and needs help fast. The call is free from any phone.
Call 911 if someone will not wake up, cannot breathe, is bleeding a lot, or is badly hurt. Call if you see a fire. If a grown-up is nearby, get them first. If not, you can call.
Do not call 911 as a joke or a test. Helpers must be free for real emergencies. The person who answers is a *dispatcher*. The dispatcher sends police, firefighters or an ambulance.

words.d: a time when someone is in danger and needs help right away
the trained person who answers 911 calls and sends help

look.prompt: Why do you think so many people call 911? Why is it important not to make joke calls?

check.q: Which is an emergency?
choices: A friend will not wake up.
check.why: Someone who will not wake up is in danger and needs help now.

check.why: A trained dispatcher answers and sends help.

choices: It costs a lot of money.

check.why: Joke calls take helpers away from people who really need them.

lessons.title: What to Say on the Call
lessons.mainIdea: On a 911 call, say what happened and where you are, answer the questions and do not hang up until told.
reading: Remember Rosa? When she called, she said what happened: Grandpa fell and could not get up. Then she gave her *address*. An address is the street name and number of a home or building.
Knowing your address is a big help. Practice saying it with a grown-up. If you are not home, look for a street sign or a store name. Say your city too.
Answer each question the dispatcher asks. Speak slowly and clearly. Do not hang up until the dispatcher says you can. The dispatcher may give *instructions*, like unlocking the door.

words.d: the street number, street name and city of a place
steps someone tells you to follow

look.title: Practice Script
look.text: Dispatcher: 911, what is your emergency? Caller: My grandpa fell and cannot get up. Dispatcher: What is your address? Caller: 412 Maple Street, Springfield. Dispatcher: Stay on the line with me.
look.prompt: Practice this script with a partner, using your own address with a grown-up's help. What two things did the caller say?

check.q: What two things should you tell the dispatcher first?
choices: What happened and where you are
check.why: The dispatcher needs to know what happened and where to send help.

check.q: What should you do if you are not home and do not know the address?
choices: Look for a street sign or store name
check.why: Street signs and store names help helpers find you.

check.q: When should you hang up?
choices: When the dispatcher says you can
check.why: Stay on the line until the dispatcher tells you it is okay.

lessons.title: Calling Poison Control
lessons.mainIdea: If someone may have swallowed or touched something harmful, an adult can call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222.
reading: Little Theo finds a bottle under the sink and takes a sip. His big sister sees. She knows cleaners can be harmful. She gets their dad right away.

Dad calls *Poison Control* at 1-800-222-1222. That number works across the United States, any time of day or night. Experts there tell callers what to do. A *poison* is something that can hurt the body if swallowed, breathed in or touched.
If the person will not wake up or cannot breathe, call 911 instead. To stay safe, never taste things you do not know. Medicines, cleaners and plant sprays should be kept up high or locked away.

words.d: a free helpline, 1-800-222-1222, with experts who say what to do about poisons
something that can hurt the body if swallowed, breathed in or touched

look.title: The Poison Help Line
look.text: The Poison Help line, 1-800-222-1222, connects callers anywhere in the United States to their local poison center. It is free and open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
look.cite: U.S. Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), Poison Help program
look.prompt: Why might it help to put this number on your refrigerator at home?

check.q: What is the Poison Control number?
check.why: Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222.

check.q: What did Theo's sister do first?
check.why: She got an adult right away.

check.q: When should you call 911 instead of Poison Control?
choices: When the person will not wake up or cannot breathe
When you want advice about lunch
check.why: If someone will not wake up or cannot breathe, it is an emergency for 911.

lessons.title: What an Allergy Is
lessons.mainIdea: An allergy is when the immune system reacts strongly to something that is harmless for most people.
reading: Omar cannot eat peanuts. For most people, peanuts are just a snack. But Omar's immune system treats peanuts like a germ. This is called an *allergy*.
Things that cause allergies are called *allergens*. Common ones are peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, bee stings and pollen. A mild reaction may be sneezing or an itchy rash.

A very strong reaction is called *anaphylaxis*. The throat may swell, and breathing can get hard. It needs help right away. Friends can help by respecting food rules and never sharing food without asking.

words.d: when the immune system reacts strongly to something harmless for most people
things that can cause an allergy, like peanuts or pollen
a very strong allergic reaction that can make breathing hard and needs help right away

look.title: Lunch Table Choices
look.text: At lunch, Kai offers Omar a cookie. Omar says, "Does it have nuts? I have a nut allergy." Kai checks the label. It says it may contain peanuts. Kai says, "Let's not risk it," and shares grapes instead.
look.prompt: How did Kai and Omar both help keep Omar safe?

check.q: What is an allergy?
choices: A strong immune reaction to something harmless for most people
check.why: An allergy is the immune system reacting to something usually harmless.

check.q: Which is a common allergen?
check.why: Peanuts are one of the common allergens listed.

check.q: What is anaphylaxis?
choices: A very strong reaction that needs help right away
check.why: Anaphylaxis is a serious reaction that can make breathing hard.

lessons.title: Epinephrine Pens
lessons.mainIdea: An epinephrine pen is medicine for a severe allergic reaction, used by adults, trained helpers or the person it belongs to.
reading: Some people with serious allergies carry an *epinephrine* pen. One well-known brand is the EpiPen. Epinephrine is a medicine that can quickly help with anaphylaxis.

The pen gives a shot, often into the outer thigh. Adults and trained helpers, like school nurses, use it. Some older kids learn to use their own pen with their doctor's help. After it is used, call 911, because the person still needs a doctor.
Your job as a friend is to know the signs and get an adult fast. Know where your friend's pen is kept. Never play with someone's pen. It is real *medicine*.

words.d: a medicine that can quickly help during a very strong allergic reaction
something used to treat or prevent sickness, given the way a doctor says

look.title: A Plan at School
look.text: Omar's school has an allergy plan. His teacher, the school nurse and the lunch staff know it. His epinephrine pen is kept in the nurse's office, and a second one goes on field trips.
look.prompt: Why is it helpful for several adults to know Omar's plan?

check.q: What is an epinephrine pen for?
check.why: Epinephrine helps quickly during anaphylaxis.

check.q: What should happen after an epinephrine pen is used?
check.why: The person still needs a doctor, so call 911.

check.q: What is a friend's main job?
choices: Know the signs and get an adult fast
check.why: Friends help by noticing signs and getting an adult quickly.

lessons.title: Staying Calm Helps
lessons.mainIdea: Taking slow breaths helps you think clearly so you can remember the steps and get help.
reading: In an emergency, your heart may race and your hands may shake. That is normal. Your body is getting ready to act. Rosa felt this too when Grandpa fell.
Slow breathing helps. Breathe in through your nose while you count to four. Breathe out slowly. One or two slow breaths help your brain *focus*. Then you can remember what to do.
Staying *calm* also helps the hurt person. A kind, steady voice helps them feel safe. You can say, "Help is coming. I am here." You do not have to fix everything. Your job is to get help.

words.d: quiet and steady, not rushed or panicked
to pay attention to one thing

look.title: Try Square Breathing
look.text: Breathe in for four counts. Hold for four counts. Breathe out for four counts. Hold for four counts. Picture tracing the four sides of a square as you go.
look.prompt: Try it twice. How does your body feel afterward? When else could this help you?

check.q: Why is it normal for your heart to race in an emergency?
choices: Your body is getting ready to act.
check.why: The reading says a racing heart is the body getting ready to act.

check.q: What helps you focus in an emergency?
check.why: Slow breaths help your brain focus.

check.q: What can you say to help a hurt person feel safe?
check.why: A kind, steady message helps the person feel safe.

lessons.title: A First-Aid Kit
lessons.mainIdea: A first-aid kit holds supplies for small hurts, and knowing where it is helps you act fast.
reading: Mr. Lopez keeps a red box in his classroom. It has a white cross on it. It is a *first-aid kit*. Inside are supplies for small hurts.
A kit often has bandages of different sizes, gauze pads, tape, and wipes for cleaning. It may have gloves, a cold pack and small scissors. Homes, schools and cars can each have one.
Know where the kit is kept at home and at school. Check it with a grown-up to replace used *supplies*. A kit does not replace a doctor. It helps with small things and gets you ready.

words.d: a box of supplies for treating small hurts
things kept ready to be used when needed

look.title: Pack a Kit
look.text: Imagine you are packing a kit for a family trip. On the table are bandages, gauze, tape, a toy car, clean wipes, gloves, a candy bar and a cold pack.
look.prompt: Which items belong in the first-aid kit? Which do not, and why?

check.why: A first-aid kit holds supplies for small hurts.

check.q: Which item is often in a first-aid kit?
check.why: Bandages are a common first-aid supply.

check.q: Why check the kit with a grown-up?

lessons.title: Helping a Friend Get an Adult
lessons.mainIdea: When a friend is hurt, one of the best ways to help is to get a trusted adult quickly.
reading: At recess, Lily falls off the monkey bars. She is crying and holding her wrist. Her friend Noah wants to help. He tells her, "Stay here. I will get the recess teacher."
Getting a *trusted adult* is often the most important step. A trusted adult is a grown-up you know can help, like a teacher, coach, nurse or parent. Noah does not try to move Lily or fix her arm.
If two friends are there, one can stay while the other runs for help. Tell the adult what happened and where. Being a good *helper* means doing your part and letting trained people do theirs.

words.d: a grown-up you know and can count on for help
someone who does their part to help another person
